glossary.Inner ear: The fluid-filled part of the ear deep in the skull, containing the cochlea and balance organs.
glossary.Vestibular system: The inner ear balance organs that sense head movement and position.
glossary.Fluctuating: Getting better and worse over time rather than staying the same.
glossary.Peripheral lesion: A problem in the inner ear or vestibular nerve rather than in the brain.
glossary.Cochlear duct: The fluid-filled tube in the cochlea containing the hearing hair cells.
glossary.Vestibular apparatus: The semicircular canals, utricle and saccule that sense balance.
glossary.Resorption: Reabsorption of fluid back into the body.
glossary.Distension: Swelling or stretching of a structure from increased pressure inside it.
glossary.Vestibular organs: The parts of the inner ear that detect head movement and gravity.
glossary.Dopamine antagonist: A drug that blocks dopamine receptors, used to stop nausea and vomiting.
glossary.D2 antagonist: A drug that blocks dopamine D2 receptors, reducing nausea and vomiting.
glossary.Antihistaminergic: Blocking histamine receptors, which helps calm the vestibular system.
glossary.Anticholinergic: Blocking acetylcholine receptors; reduces vestibular signalling but causes dry mouth and drowsiness.
glossary.Histamine analogue: A drug with a similar structure to histamine that acts on its receptors.
glossary.H1 agonist: A drug that stimulates histamine H1 receptors.
glossary.H3 antagonist: A drug that blocks histamine H3 receptors, increasing histamine release.
glossary.Cochlear blood flow: Blood supply to the cochlea; betahistine is thought to increase it.
glossary.Vestibular nerve: The nerve carrying balance signals from the inner ear to the brainstem.
glossary.MRI brain: A detailed scan of the brain using magnets, used here to exclude a tumour.
glossary.Low salt diet: Cutting dietary sodium, thought to reduce endolymph volume.
glossary.Debilitating: So severe it stops normal daily activity.
